JO 7110.65 §2-4-3 requires verifying the following when a pilot reads back an ATC clearance:

- Ensure all items in the clearance are correctly read back.
- Ensure hold short instructions, whether part of taxi instructions or a LAHSO clearance, are correctly read back.
- Ensure the pilot uses the call sign or registration number in the read back, acknowledging the clearance or instruction.

For example, if the clearance is "Cleared to land Runway 18, report touchdown," the pilot should read back "Cleared to land Runway 18, report touchdown." If the clearance includes a hold short instruction, such as "Hold short of Runway 18," the pilot should read back "Hold short of Runway 18." Always confirm the call sign or registration number is included in the read back to ensure clear and accurate communication.

Wake turbulence procedures apply under JO 7110.65 when an aircraft is operating behind another aircraft and requires wake turbulence separation. According to JO 7110.65 §2-1-19, these procedures must be applied. The specific conditions and procedures are detailed in:

- JO 7110.65 §2-1-19 (Wake Turbulence)
- JO 7110.65 §2-1-20 (Wake Turbulence Cautionary Advisories)

JO 7110.65 §3-9-6 (Departure Procedures and Separation) is the relevant section. Don't clear a departing aircraft for takeoff behind another until the preceding aircraft has departed and crossed the runway end or turned to avert any conflict. The phraseology is: "The preceding aircraft has departed and crossed the runway end or turned to avert any conflict. Cleared for takeoff." Refer to §3-9-6 for more details.

JO 7110.65 §3-10-3 governs this scenario. The arriving aircraft may cross the landing threshold behind another aircraft on the same runway if:

- The preceding aircraft has landed and is clear of the runway.
- Between sunrise and sunset, if you can determine distances by suitable landmarks, the minimum distances from the landing threshold must be maintained:

  - 3,000 feet for a Category I aircraft behind a Category I or II.
  - 4,500 feet for a Category II aircraft behind a Category I or II.
  - 6,000 feet for either aircraft behind a Category III.

These conditions apply when visual separation is used. If the preceding aircraft has departed and crossed the runway end, the arriving aircraft may cross the threshold if the minimum distance is maintained.

JO 7110.65 §4-2-1 specifies the order for IFR clearances. The order is:

- Aircraft identification.
- Clearance limit.

If the clearance limit is an airport, "airport" follows the airport name.

For example: "Delta 123, cleared IFR to Chicago O'Hare Airport, expect radar vectors to the VOR, maintain 3000."

JO 7110.65 §4-5-1 covers vertical separation. Up to and including FL 410, the minimum is 1,000 feet. Above FL 410, the minimum is 2,000 feet between non-RVSM aircraft and all other aircraft at or above FL 290. For aircraft above FL 600, the separation is 5,000 feet between military aircraft.

Chapter 5 §5-5-4 (Radar Separation Minimums) specifies the standard radar separation minimums in terminal airspace for single-sensor ASR. When less than 40 miles from the antenna, the minimum is 3 miles. When 40 miles or more from the antenna, the minimum is 5 miles. For single sensor monopulse secondary surveillance radar (MSSR), when less than 60 miles from the antenna, the minimum is 3 miles.

— JO 7110.65 §5-5-4

The transferring controller must verbally obtain the receiving controller’s approval before making any changes to an aircraft’s flight path, altitude, speed, or data block information during the handoff process. This is specified in JO 7110.65 §5-4-5(b).

Chapter 5, §5-10-11 of JO 7110.65 states that before an aircraft starts final descent for a full stop landing and weather reports indicate that any portion of the final approach will be conducted in IFR conditions, you must issue the specific missed approach procedure approved for the radar approach being conducted. This ensures the pilot has clear instructions on what to do if the approach cannot be completed safely.

JO 7110.65 §7-9-2 — VFR aircraft must obtain an ATC clearance to operate in Class B airspace. The prescribed phraseology is "CLEARED THROUGH/TO ENTER/OUT OF BRAVO AIRSPACE," and as appropriate, "VIA (route). MAINTAIN (altitude) WHILE IN BRAVO AIRSPACE." The clearance is explicit — "radar contact" alone doesn't authorize entry.
JO 7110.65 §7-3-1 says you may clear an IFR aircraft to maintain VFR-on-top if the pilot requests it. No other conditions are specified.

JO 7110.65 §10-1-1 — an emergency is either a Distress or an Urgency condition, as defined in the Pilot/Controller Glossary. Distress means immediate assistance is required to save life or property, and a pilot declares it by saying "Mayday," preferably repeated three times. Urgency is a safety concern not yet immediately life-threatening, and a pilot declares it by saying "Pan-Pan," also preferably repeated three times. Both "Mayday" and "Pan-Pan" signal the nature of the emergency to the controller.
